[RAZI-FULL:v29p161#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Tasbih is inward belief that God is one, without partner, and able rather than incapable of resurrection, or verbal praise such as “Subhan Allah,” or equivalent words.

[RAZI-FULL:v29p161#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi distinguishes the epithets: perceptible greatness suggests nearness to all, while absolute elevation suggests remoteness from everything; God transcends perception, and positive attributes exceed what knowledge reaches. | mentions 87:1

[RAZI-FULL:v29p161/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, bāʾ is meaningful: idolaters concede God created everything but call idols gods by name, so they must not assign the divine name to anything besides Him; the admonition addresses any hearer.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p161/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, the command is to glorify God by naming Him aloud among one's people, describing Him and continuing to preach even if they refuse; a purely inward tasbih would not convey this.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p161/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Razi also allows taking the phrase as beginning with the name of the Lord, making bāʾ nonredundant.
[QURTUBI-FULL:56:73-74/r14] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The command to glorify God’s great name repudiates the partners and inability to resurrect that idolaters attribute to Him.

I’m keeping the reported bowing instruction and the smaller grammatical and contemplative views visible as distinct positions.
